remaining_gaps: Effect of the Career Compensation Act of 1949 (63 Stat. 802) on this order's authorities is not resolved by pinned evidence. The held statute text (jobs/source-ladder/output/texts/queue_EO_10061_Career_Compensation_Act_of_1949_Pub._L._81-351_63_Stat._802_Pay_Readjustment_Act_of_1_8558d6ea73.txt, not an evidence id in this packet's dossier) repeals the Pay Readjustment Act of 1942 on which this order's amended regulation rests (section 531(b)(34), effective October 1, 1949 under section 533(a), with the travel-status part of section 10(1) and section 12 repealed by section 531(c)(12), effective January 1, 1950 under section 533(c)), and section 303 moves travel and per diem allowances to regulations of the Secretaries concerned.

Executive Order 10084 (adopting existing regulations under the repealed act as presidential regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act) and its amendments Executive Orders 10098 and 10118 (cease dates of January 31, 1950, March 31, 1950, and June 30, 1950 only for sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d); section 303 is not among the continued sections) bear on whether Part D and the amended Executive Order No. 9871 survived to this order's own June 30, 1950 sunset. None of these instruments names Executive Order 10061 or Executive Order No. 9871, so under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 on unnamed instruments they are disclosed earlier candidate ends and not ends; that ruling requires the candidate source to be pinned.

Missing source: a source supplement for this packet pinning the Career Compensation Act of 1949 excerpts (sections 303, 531 and 533) and the texts of Executive Orders 10084, 10098 and 10118 as evidence ids, so the claim can record them as pinned earlier candidate ends and analyse whether each extinguished Part D before June 30, 1950. Without those pins the claim cannot disclose the candidate ends the ruling requires, and the own-terms end of June 30, 1950 cannot be shown to be the first end.

The provisional NO conflicts with held evidence that is not resolved: the dossier's conflict NO_ORDER_IN_FORCE_ON_1989_01_20 records that the Office of the Federal Register 1989 Codification (chapter 32, National Defense; jobs/ofr-codification-1989/output/texts/EO_10295.txt) prints this order as in force on January 20, 1989, 38 years after the September 28, 1951 signing date the earlier draft treated as an end, and the dossier's status-history flags (empty catalog note does not establish current effect; post-snapshot end basis not located) show no ending candidate after that day.

The order makes the described design 'a part of this order' and approves it as the official seal of the United States Court of Military Appeals; the only legal basis for the seal's official status that any held source shows is this order, and no held source shows that a later instrument, statute, court rule or the Court's renaming ended or replaced that designation, so an end date for the approval clause cannot be supported.

Missing source: a held current or post-1989 source on the official seal of the United States Court of Military Appeals (now the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces) showing either that this order's designation was superseded, revoked or otherwise ended (with its date and actor) or that it continues; neither the current-law searches (no U.S. Code or eCFR mention of this order) nor the later-events catalog supplies one.

Executive Order 10441 (signed March 31, 1953; 18 FR 1824; held text jobs/fr-originals/output/texts/EO_10441.txt) continues in effect until and including July 1, 1953 the appointments of Army and Air Force officers and warrant officers who are missing, captured or interned and whose appointments would terminate under the same three listed provisions of law after April 27, 1952 and before July 1, 1953; it carries part of the appointments this order continued past this order's own end of April 1, 1953. Under the production route and the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 that further continuation is a later event with its own date and quote, not an end of this order, and the earlier draft's statement that no held order extends this order is wrong.

Executive Order 10441 does not cite this order's number, the packet's later-event chain for this order is empty and its citable-evidence list holds no record for that order, so the packet cannot record it as a later event with a pinned source; the number-only, catalog and current-law searches were not adequate for a serial continuation order with a nearly identical title.

Missing source: a source supplement pinning the text of Executive Order 10441 (18 FR 1824) as an evidence id for this order so that it can be entered as a later event, and a search for any other serial continuation of the same appointments after April 1, 1953 by subject and statute (section 1(c) of the Emergency Powers Continuation Act, 66 Stat. 333) and not only by this order's number.

The second paragraph directs the heads of departments, agencies and independent establishments, to the extent consistent with the needs of the service, to adopt a liberal policy for granting annual leave to all employees who wish to take such leave over 'the holiday period'. The order does not define that period or equate it with Friday, December 26, 1958 (all covered employees were already excused that day and Christmas Day is itself a holiday, so the direction operates on other days), and no held source dates its end.

The first paragraph (excusal from duty all day on December 26, 1958, with its holiday treatment) and the third paragraph (national-security exclusion) have the stated day as their own-terms end, but the first end of the leave-policy direction cannot be shown by evidence: reading it as tied to December 26, 1958 would be a convenient reading, not one the text or any held source supports, and no later order, circular or notice in the held corpus ends or dates it (the number searches, the Federal Register disposition-note search and the current-law searches have no hit for this order, and Executive Order 12553 has no entry for it).

Missing source: a held source (for example a Civil Service Commission or agency leave notice for the 1958 holiday season) that dates the 'holiday period' the leave direction refers to, or other evidence that the direction was performed or lapsed on a date; without it the clause has no supportable first-end date, so the whole-order end date cannot be fixed.

Section 4's last sentence, which requests the heads of departments and agencies to arrange their affairs so that employees can be excused on July 3, 1959 'or' given compensatory time in lieu of the excused day without additional appropriations, has no end that held evidence supports: compensatory time in lieu of an excused day is by nature given on a later day, the order states no deadline for it, and no held source shows the request was spent or lapsed at the close of July 3, 1959 (the surviving text of that sentence is also damaged in the held text layer, and the American Presidency Project transcription is not a registered source for it).

Section 1(b) excuses an employee whose workday 'commences on July 2 or July 3, 1959' from his entire workday; a workday commencing on July 3 runs into July 4, 1959, so the excusal can operate after the close of July 3, and the earlier draft's close-of-July-3 end for section 1 is not supported. Section 3 runs to the end of fiscal year 1960, a date the order does not state and that rests on the statutory fiscal-year definition, which is not a held text.

Because the compensatory-time request has no established end, the latest first end among the clauses, and so the whole-order end date, is not established by the held sources. Missing source: a held source dating the use or lapse of the compensatory-time arrangement for July 3, 1959 (for example a Civil Service Commission or agency circular implementing the order), and a held statement of the fiscal-year 1960 end date for section 3.

The leave-policy sentence directs the heads of departments, agencies and independent establishments, to the extent consistent with the needs of the service, to adopt a liberal policy for granting annual leave to all employees who wish to take such leave over 'the holiday period'. The order describes December 24, 1959 as the day preceding Christmas Day, so any reading of the holiday period includes at least Christmas Day, December 25, 1959; the direction cannot have ended at the close of December 24, 1959, as the earlier draft recorded, and no held source dates the period's end.

The excusal paragraph and the national-security exclusion are tied to the stated half-day of December 24, 1959, but the first end of the leave-policy direction (two spans of one sentence, split by a Register page break) is not shown by any held source: no later order, circular or notice in the held corpus dates or ends it, the number searches, the disposition-note search and the current-law searches have no hit for this order, and Executive Order 12553 has no entry for it. The whole-order end date, which must equal the latest clause end, therefore cannot be fixed.

Missing source: a held source (for example a Civil Service Commission or agency leave notice for the 1959 holiday season) that dates the 'holiday period' referred to in the leave sentence, or other evidence that the direction was performed or lapsed on a date.
